P1● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

Which pair of figures is not always similar?

similar polygons need equal angles and proportional sides (Topic 2). Why it applies: a counter-example shows "not always".

All circles are similar.
All angles are 60° and all side ratios equal.
Rectangles can have different length-to-width ratios.
All angles are 90° and all side ratios equal.

Given: four kinds of pairs. Asked: the pair that can fail to be similar.

Concept used: similar polygons need equal angles and proportional sides (Topic 2). Why it applies: a counter-example shows "not always".

  1. 1

    Two rectangles 2 cm × 3 cm and 2 cm × 5 cm: all angles 90°, but 22≠53\dfrac{2}{2} \neq \dfrac{5}{3}22​=35​.

  2. 2

    Circles, equilateral triangles and squares always have the same shape.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (c) ✔ Rectangles can have different length-to-width ratios.
    • (a) ✘ All circles are similar.
    • (b) ✘ All angles are 60° and all side ratios equal.
    • (d) ✘ All angles are 90° and all side ratios equal.

  3. Check: a 2 × 3 rectangle is "short and wide", a 2 × 5 one is "long and thin" — different shapes ✔.

  4. Answer (c)

    Common trap: Choosing (d) because squares "can be of different sizes". Different size does not stop figures being similar.

angle sum, AA and the matching card (Topic 4). Why it applies: the order must pair equal angles.

It claims ∠A=∠X\angle A = \angle X∠A=∠X: 50° = 70°.
△ABC ~ △YZX.
It claims ∠A=∠Z\angle A = \angle Z∠A=∠Z: 50° = 60°.
It claims ∠B=∠X\angle B = \angle X∠B=∠X: 60° = 70°.

Concept used: angle sum, AA and the matching card (Topic 4). Why it applies: the order must pair equal angles.

    ∠C=180°−50°−60°=70°\angle C = 180° - 50° - 60° = 70°∠C=180°−50°−60°=70°; ∠Z=180°−70°−50°=60°\angle Z = 180° - 70° - 50° = 60°∠Z=180°−70°−50°=60°.

P4● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

In △ABC and △PQR, ABPQ=ACPR\dfrac{AB}{PQ} = \dfrac{AC}{PR}PQAB​=PRAC​ and ∠B=∠Q\angle B = \angle Q∠B=∠Q. Which statement is correct?

SAS needs the equal angles between the proportional sides (Topic 4). Why it applies: AB and AC meet at A, not at B.

SAS would need ∠A=∠P\angle A = \angle P∠A=∠P.
Only one pair of angles is known.
Only two side ratios are known.
The angle is not included.

Given: two side ratios and one pair of equal angles. Asked: which criterion, if any.

Concept used: SAS needs the equal angles between the proportional sides (Topic 4). Why it applies: AB and AC meet at A, not at B.

  1. 1

    Sides AB and AC form ∠A\angle A∠A; sides PQ and PR form ∠P\angle P∠P.

  2. 2

    The equal angles given are ∠B\angle B∠B and ∠Q\angle Q∠Q — not the included angles.

  3. 3

    AA needs two angle pairs, SSS needs three side ratios. Nothing applies.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (d) ✔ The angle is not included.
    • (a) ✘ SAS would need ∠A=∠P\angle A = \angle P∠A=∠P.
    • (b) ✘ Only one pair of angles is known.
    • (c) ✘ Only two side ratios are known.

  4. Check: Topic 4, Worked example 3 (b) shows such a pair that is not similar ✔.

  5. Answer (d)

    Common trap: Choosing (a) because "one angle and two sides" are given.
P5● FoundationVery short answer · 1 markOriginal

A girl 1.2 m tall casts a shadow 0.9 m long. At the same time, a tree casts a shadow 6.3 m long. How tall is the tree?

Full solution

Given: girl 1.2 m, her shadow 0.9 m; tree's shadow 6.3 m. Asked: the tree's height h.

Concept used: each height with its own shadow (Topic 5). Why it applies: the sun's rays make equal angles at the shadow tips, so the triangles are similar (AA).

  1. 1

    1.20.9=h6.3\dfrac{1.2}{0.9} = \dfrac{h}{6.3}0.91.2​=6.3h​.

  2. 2

    Multiply by 6.3: h=1.2×6.30.9=8.4h = \dfrac{1.2 \times 6.3}{0.9} = 8.4h=0.91.2×6.3​=8.4 m.

  3. Check: each height is 43\dfrac{4}{3}34​ of its shadow: 43×6.3=8.4\dfrac{4}{3} \times 6.3 = 8.434​×6.3=8.4 ✔.

  4. Answer 8.4 m

    Common trap: 1.26.3=h0.9\dfrac{1.2}{6.3} = \dfrac{h}{0.9}6.31.2​=0.9h​ — the girl's height over the tree's shadow — gives about 0.17 m.

P6● FoundationVery short answer · 1 markOriginal

In △PQR, A is on PQ and B is on PR with PA=6PA = 6PA=6 cm, AQ=9AQ = 9AQ=9 cm, PB=4PB = 4PB=4 cm and BR=7BR = 7BR=7 cm. Is AB∥QRAB \parallel QRAB∥QR?

Full solution

Given: the four pieces. Asked: parallel or not.

Concept used: BPT and its converse (Topic 3). Why it applies: parallel exactly when the two ratios are equal.

  1. 1

    PAAQ=69=23\dfrac{PA}{AQ} = \dfrac{6}{9} = \dfrac{2}{3}AQPA​=96​=32​; PBBR=47\dfrac{PB}{BR} = \dfrac{4}{7}BRPB​=74​.

  2. 2

    23≠47\dfrac{2}{3} \neq \dfrac{4}{7}32​=74​ (14≠1214 \neq 1214=12), so AB is not parallel to QR.

  3. Check: if AB∥QRAB \parallel QRAB∥QR, then BR would be 32×4=6\dfrac{3}{2} \times 4 = 623​×4=6 cm, not 7 cm ✔.

  4. Answer No

    Common trap: Saying "yes" because both ratios are "about 0.6".

P7● FoundationVery short answer · 1 markOriginal

The sides of a triangle are 4 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm. The longest side of a similar triangle is 15 cm. Find its perimeter.

Full solution

Given: sides 4, 5, 6 (cm); the matching longest side is 15 cm. Asked: the perimeter of the second triangle.

Concept used: perimeters are in the side ratio (Topic 5). Why it applies: longest side matches longest side.

  1. 1

    Scale factor 156=2.5\dfrac{15}{6} = 2.5615​=2.5.

  2. 2

    Perimeter =2.5×(4+5+6)=2.5×15=37.5= 2.5 \times (4 + 5 + 6) = 2.5 \times 15 = 37.5=2.5×(4+5+6)=2.5×15=37.5 cm.

  3. Check: sides 10, 12.5, 15 add to 37.5 ✔.

  4. Answer 37.5 cm

    Common trap: Using 154\dfrac{15}{4}415​ (pairing 15 with the shortest side).

P8● FoundationTrue/False with justification · 1 markOriginal

True or false? "All right-angled triangles are similar." Justify.

Full solution

Given: a claim about all right triangles. Asked: true or false, with a reason.

Concept used: one counter-example disproves "all" (Topics 2 and 4). Why it applies: right triangles can have different acute angles.

  1. 1

    A right triangle with angles 90°, 45°, 45° and one with angles 90°, 30°, 60°.

  2. 2

    Their angles do not match, so they are not similar.

  3. Check: AA would need a second pair of equal angles; 45° matches neither 30° nor 60° ✔.

  4. Answer False — e.g. a 90°–45°–45° triangle and a 90°–30°–60° triangle are not similar.

    Common trap: "They all have a right angle, so AA." One equal angle is not two.

P9● FoundationVery short answer · 1 markOriginal

△ABC ~ △DEF with AB=6AB = 6AB=6 cm, DE=4DE = 4DE=4 cm and BC=9BC = 9BC=9 cm. Find EF.

Full solution

Given: △ABC ~ △DEF, AB=6AB = 6AB=6, DE=4DE = 4DE=4, BC=9BC = 9BC=9 (cm). Asked: EF.

Concept used: corresponding sides are proportional (Topic 4). Why it applies: BC matches EF (last two letters).

  1. 1

    EFBC=DEAB=46=23\dfrac{EF}{BC} = \dfrac{DE}{AB} = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}BCEF​=ABDE​=64​=32​.

  2. 2

    EF=23×9=6EF = \dfrac{2}{3} \times 9 = 6EF=32​×9=6 cm.

  3. Check: 46=69\dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{6}{9}64​=96​ ✔.

  4. Answer 6 cm

    Common trap: Multiplying by 32\dfrac{3}{2}23​ (13.5 cm) — △DEF is the smaller triangle.

P10●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

In △ABC, DE∥BCDE \parallel BCDE∥BC with D on AB and E on AC. AD=4AD = 4AD=4 cm, DB=6DB = 6DB=6 cm and AC=12.5AC = 12.5AC=12.5 cm. Find AE and EC.

Full solution

Given: DE∥BCDE \parallel BCDE∥BC, AD=4AD = 4AD=4, DB=6DB = 6DB=6, AC=12.5AC = 12.5AC=12.5 (cm). Asked: AE, EC.

Concept used: BPT; then splitting a length in a ratio (Topics 1 and 3). Why it applies: AE : EC = AD : DB.

  1. 1

    AEEC=ADDB=46=23\dfrac{AE}{EC} = \dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}ECAE​=DBAD​=64​=32​.

  2. 2

    AC has 2+3=52 + 3 = 52+3=5 parts; one part is 12.5÷5=2.512.5 \div 5 = 2.512.5÷5=2.5 cm.

  3. 3

    AE=2×2.5=5AE = 2 \times 2.5 = 5AE=2×2.5=5 cm and EC=3×2.5=7.5EC = 3 \times 2.5 = 7.5EC=3×2.5=7.5 cm.

  4. Check: ADAB=410=512.5\dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{4}{10} = \dfrac{5}{12.5}ABAD​=104​=12.55​ ✔.

  5. Answer AE=5AE = 5AE=5 cm, EC=7.5EC = 7.5EC=7.5 cm

    Common trap: AE=23×12.5AE = \dfrac{2}{3} \times 12.5AE=32​×12.5 — using the part-to-part ratio on the whole side.

P11●● StandardProof · 3 marksOriginal

In △PQR, X is a point on PQ and Y is a point on PR such that ∠PXY=∠PRQ\angle PXY = \angle PRQ∠PXY=∠PRQ. (a) Prove that △PXY ~ △PRQ. (b) If PX=4PX = 4PX=4 cm, PR=10PR = 10PR=10 cm and PY=5PY = 5PY=5 cm, find PQ.

Full solution

Given: ∠PXY=∠PRQ\angle PXY = \angle PRQ∠PXY=∠PRQ. To prove: △PXY ~ △PRQ; then find PQ.

Concept used: AA with the common angle P; the matching card (Topic 4). Why it applies: the given equal angles are at X and at R, so X ↔ R.

  1. Statement Reason
    1. In △PXY and △PRQ: ∠XPY=∠RPQ\angle XPY = \angle RPQ∠XPY=∠RPQ Common angle P
    2. ∠PXY=∠PRQ\angle PXY = \angle PRQ∠PXY=∠PRQ Given
    3. △PXY ~ △PRQ AA similarity criterion (P↔PP \leftrightarrow PP↔P, X↔RX \leftrightarrow RX↔R, Y↔QY \leftrightarrow QY↔Q)
    4. PXPR=PYPQ\dfrac{PX}{PR} = \dfrac{PY}{PQ}PRPX​=PQPY​ Corresponding sides (first two letters; first and last letters)
  2. 5

    (b)

    410=5PQ\dfrac{4}{10} = \dfrac{5}{PQ}104​=PQ5​.

  3. 6

    Cross-multiply: 4×PQ=504 \times PQ = 504×PQ=50, so PQ=12.5PQ = 12.5PQ=12.5 cm.

  4. Check: PXPR=0.4=512.5\dfrac{PX}{PR} = 0.4 = \dfrac{5}{12.5}PRPX​=0.4=12.55​ ✔; X lies on PQ since 4<12.54 < 12.54<12.5, and Y on PR since 5<105 < 105<10 ✔.

  5. Answer (a) △PXY ~ △PRQ (AA) (b) PQ=12.5PQ = 12.5PQ=12.5 cm

    Common trap: Writing △PXY ~ △PQR and then PXPQ=PYPR\dfrac{PX}{PQ} = \dfrac{PY}{PR}PQPX​=PRPY​, which gives PQ=8PQ = 8PQ=8 cm — wrong.

P12●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

In △ABC, DE∥BCDE \parallel BCDE∥BC with D on AB and E on AC. If AD:DB=3:5AD : DB = 3 : 5AD:DB=3:5 and BC=16BC = 16BC=16 cm, find DE.

Full solution

Given: DE∥BCDE \parallel BCDE∥BC, AD:DB=3:5AD : DB = 3 : 5AD:DB=3:5, BC=16BC = 16BC=16 cm. Asked: DE.

Concept used: △ADE ~ △ABC (AA, corresponding angles); the ratio uses the whole side AB (Topics 4 and 5). Why it applies: DE and BC are matching sides.

  1. 1

    △ADE ~ △ABC, so DEBC=ADAB\dfrac{DE}{BC} = \dfrac{AD}{AB}BCDE​=ABAD​.

  2. 2

    AB is 3+5=83 + 5 = 83+5=8 parts, so ADAB=38\dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{3}{8}ABAD​=83​.

  3. 3

    DE=38×16=6DE = \dfrac{3}{8} \times 16 = 6DE=83​×16=6 cm.

  4. Check: DE is shorter than BC, as it must be ✔.

  5. Answer DE=6DE = 6DE=6 cm

    Common trap: DE=35×16=9.6DE = \dfrac{3}{5} \times 16 = 9.6DE=53​×16=9.6 cm — DB is not a side of either triangle.

P13●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

Here is part of a student's proof of BPT for △ABC with DE∥BCDE \parallel BCDE∥BC:

"ar(ADE)ar(BDE)=ADDB\dfrac{\text{ar}(ADE)}{\text{ar}(BDE)} = \dfrac{AD}{DB}ar(BDE)ar(ADE)​=DBAD​ and ar(ADE)ar(DEC)=AEEC\dfrac{\text{ar}(ADE)}{\text{ar}(DEC)} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}ar(DEC)ar(ADE)​=ECAE​. Since △BDE and △DEC have the same base DE, ar(BDE) = ar(DEC). So ADDB=AEEC\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}DBAD​=ECAE​."

Name two things a marking scheme would take marks off for, and write the correct versions.

Full solution

Given: a proof with gaps. Asked: two gaps and their corrections.

Concept used: the full BPT proof (Topic 3). Why it applies: the schemes award marks for the figure, construction, the area ratios with heights, and the reason for equal areas.

  1. 1

    No construction or heights: the two ratios appear with no reason. Correct: "Construction: join BE and CD; draw EN⊥ABEN \perp ABEN⊥AB and DM⊥ACDM \perp ACDM⊥AC. ar(ADE)=12×AD×EN\text{ar}(ADE) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times AD \times ENar(ADE)=21​×AD×EN and ar(BDE)=12×DB×EN\text{ar}(BDE) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times DB \times ENar(BDE)=21​×DB×EN, so ar(ADE)ar(BDE)=ADDB\dfrac{\text{ar}(ADE)}{\text{ar}(BDE)} = \dfrac{AD}{DB}ar(BDE)ar(ADE)​=DBAD​" (similarly with DM).

  2. 2

    Incomplete reason for equal areas: "same base" alone does not fix the heights. Correct: "△BDE and △DEC are on the same base DE and between the same parallels DE and BC, so ar(BDE) = ar(DEC)."

  3. Check: compare with the scheme of SQP 2025-26 Basic Q32, which gives separate marks for the construction, each area ratio, and the equal-area step ✔.

  4. Answer (1) missing construction and heights (EN, DM) behind the two area ratios; (2) the equal-area reason must include "between the same parallels DE and BC". (Also acceptable: no figure; no "Given / To prove".)

    Common trap: Thinking the proof is fine because the conclusion is right. Marks go to the reasons.

P14●● StandardTrue/False with justification · 2 marksOriginal

In △ABC, D is on AB and E is on AC with AD=2AD = 2AD=2 cm, DB=3DB = 3DB=3 cm, AE=3AE = 3AE=3 cm and EC=4EC = 4EC=4 cm. Priya says: "DE looks parallel to BC in my sketch, so △ADE ~ △ABC and DEBC=25\dfrac{DE}{BC} = \dfrac{2}{5}BCDE​=52​." Is she right? Justify.

Full solution

Given: the four pieces; Priya's claim. Asked: right or wrong, with a reason.

Concept used: the converse of BPT decides parallel lines; never assume (Topics 3 and 4). Why it applies: her whole argument rests on "parallel".

  1. 1

    ADDB=23\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{2}{3}DBAD​=32​ and AEEC=34\dfrac{AE}{EC} = \dfrac{3}{4}ECAE​=43​ — not equal (8≠98 \neq 98=9).

  2. 2

    So DE is not parallel to BC (if it were, BPT would make the ratios equal).

  3. 3

    Also ADAB=25\dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{2}{5}ABAD​=52​ but AEAC=37\dfrac{AE}{AC} = \dfrac{3}{7}ACAE​=73​: the sides around ∠A\angle A∠A are not proportional, so SAS does not give △ADE ~ △ABC either.

  4. Check: a sketch drawn to scale shows DE slightly tilted ✔.

  5. Answer She is wrong: 23≠34\dfrac{2}{3} \neq \dfrac{3}{4}32​=43​, so DE is not parallel to BC, the triangles are not shown similar, and DEBC=25\dfrac{DE}{BC} = \dfrac{2}{5}BCDE​=52​ does not follow.

    Common trap: Trusting a sketch. "Looks parallel" is not a reason.

P15●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

A lamp is 6.3 m above the ground on a vertical pole. A woman 1.8 m tall stands 5 m from the foot of the pole. Find the length of her shadow.

Full solution

Given: lamp 6.3 m, woman 1.8 m, distance from the pole 5 m. Asked: shadow x.

Concept used: AA (right angles, common angle at the shadow tip); big base = distance + shadow (Topic 5). Why it applies: lamp, head and shadow tip are on one ray.

  1. 1

    Let AB be the pole, CD the woman, E the shadow tip, DE=xDE = xDE=x. △ABE ~ △CDE (AA).

  2. 2

    BEDE=ABCD\dfrac{BE}{DE} = \dfrac{AB}{CD}DEBE​=CDAB​, so 5+xx=6.31.8=3.5\dfrac{5 + x}{x} = \dfrac{6.3}{1.8} = 3.5x5+x​=1.86.3​=3.5.

  3. 3

    Multiply by x: 5+x=3.5x5 + x = 3.5x5+x=3.5x.

  4. 4

    Subtract x: 5=2.5x5 = 2.5x5=2.5x, so x=2x = 2x=2 m.

  5. Check: 5+22=3.5\dfrac{5 + 2}{2} = 3.525+2​=3.5 ✔.

  6. Answer The shadow is 2 m long.

    Common trap: 5x=3.5\dfrac{5}{x} = 3.5x5​=3.5 (forgetting that the big base includes the shadow) gives about 1.43 m.

P17●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

In △ABC, AB=6AB = 6AB=6 cm, BC=8BC = 8BC=8 cm and CA=10CA = 10CA=10 cm. In △PQR, PQ=12PQ = 12PQ=12 cm, QR=9QR = 9QR=9 cm and RP=15RP = 15RP=15 cm. Show that the triangles are similar, write the correspondence, and find ∠Q\angle Q∠Q if ∠B=90°\angle B = 90°∠B=90°.

Full solution

Given: three sides of each; ∠B=90°\angle B = 90°∠B=90°. Asked: similarity, correspondence, ∠Q\angle Q∠Q.

Concept used: SSS, matched shortest with shortest (Topic 4). Why it applies: only sides are given.

  1. 1

    Order: △ABC: 6 (AB), 8 (BC), 10 (CA). △PQR: 9 (QR), 12 (PQ), 15 (RP).

P26●●● AdvancedShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

In △ABC, DE∥BCDE \parallel BCDE∥BC with D on AB and E on AC. AD=x−2AD = x - 2AD=x−2, DB=2x−1DB = 2x - 1DB=2x−1, AE=x−3AE = x - 3AE=x−3 and EC=x+1EC = x + 1EC=x+1 (all in cm). Find x and the four lengths.

Full solution

Given: DE∥BCDE \parallel BCDE∥BC and the four lengths. Asked: x.

Concept used: BPT, cross-multiplication and a quadratic (Topic 3; Chapter 4); reject a root that makes a length negative. Why it applies: this time the x2x^2x2 terms do not cancel, so there are two roots to test.

  1. 1

    x−22x−1=x−3x+1\dfrac{x - 2}{2x - 1} = \dfrac{x - 3}{x + 1}2x−1x−2​=x+1x−3​.

  2. 2

    Cross-multiply: (x−2)(x+1)=(2x−1)(x−3)(x - 2)(x + 1) = (2x - 1)(x - 3)(x−2)(x+1)=(2x−1)(x−3).

  3. 3

    Expand: x2−x−2=2x2−7x+3x^2 - x - 2 = 2x^2 - 7x + 3x2−x−2=2x2−7x+3.

  4. 4

    Bring everything to one side: x2−6x+5=0x^2 - 6x + 5 = 0x2−6x+5=0.

  5. 5

    Factorise: (x−1)(x−5)=0(x - 1)(x - 5) = 0(x−1)(x−5)=0, so x=1x = 1x=1 or x=5x = 5x=5.

  6. 6

    x=1x = 1x=1 makes AD=−1AD = -1AD=−1 and AE=−2AE = -2AE=−2 — impossible. So x=5x = 5x=5: AD=3AD = 3AD=3, DB=9DB = 9DB=9, AE=2AE = 2AE=2, EC=6EC = 6EC=6 (cm).

  7. Check: 39=26=13\dfrac{3}{9} = \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}93​=62​=31​ ✔.

  8. Answer x=5x = 5x=5; AD=3AD = 3AD=3 cm, DB=9DB = 9DB=9 cm, AE=2AE = 2AE=2 cm, EC=6EC = 6EC=6 cm

    Common trap: Keeping x=1x = 1x=1 because it solves the equation. It does, but it makes two lengths negative. Test every root in every length.

P28●●● AdvancedShort answer · 4 marksOriginal

Two vertical poles, 6 m and 9 m tall, stand 15 m apart on level ground. A wire runs from the top of each pole to the foot of the other. At what height above the ground do the wires cross?

Concept used: two pairs of similar triangles (AA), then adding fractions (Topic 5). Why it applies: the perpendicular from P to the ground is parallel to both poles.

    Let PM be the perpendicular from P to BD; PM=hPM = hPM=h, BM=pBM = pBM=p, MD=qMD = qMD=q, p+q=15p + q = 15p+q=15.

    △DMP ~ △DBA (AA: right angles at M and B, common angle D), so h6=q15\dfrac{h}{6} = \dfrac{q}{15}6h​=15q​.

  3. 3

    △BMP ~ △BDC (AA: right angles at M and D, common angle B), so h9=p15\dfrac{h}{9} = \dfrac{p}{15}9h​=15p​.

  4. 4

    Add: h6+h9=p+q15=1\dfrac{h}{6} + \dfrac{h}{9} = \dfrac{p + q}{15} = 16h​+9h​=15p+q​=1.

  5. 5

    3h+2h18=1\dfrac{3h + 2h}{18} = 1183h+2h​=1, so 5h=185h = 185h=18 and h=3.6h = 3.6h=3.6 m.

  6. Check: q=15×3.66=9q = 15 \times \dfrac{3.6}{6} = 9q=15×63.6​=9 and p=15×3.69=6p = 15 \times \dfrac{3.6}{9} = 6p=15×93.6​=6: p+q=15p + q = 15p+q=15 ✔.

  7. Answer The wires cross 3.6 m above the ground.

P29●●● AdvancedShort answer · 4 marksOriginal

A man 1.8 m tall stands 2 m from the foot of a lamp-post and finds that his shadow is 1 m long. He then walks straight away from the post until he is 5 m from it. (a) How high is the lamp? (b) How long is his shadow now?

Full solution

Given: man 1.8 m; at 2 m from the post the shadow is 1 m; then he is 5 m from the post. Asked: the lamp's height H, then the new shadow s.

Concept used: the lamp-post set-up twice (Topic 5). Why it applies: both positions give a small triangle inside a big one with the same shadow tip.

  1. 1

    First position: big base 2+1=32 + 1 = 32+1=3 m. H1.8=31\dfrac{H}{1.8} = \dfrac{3}{1}1.8H​=13​, so H=5.4H = 5.4H=5.4 m.

  2. 2

    Second position: 5+ss=5.41.8=3\dfrac{5 + s}{s} = \dfrac{5.4}{1.8} = 3s5+s​=1.85.4​=3.

  3. 3

    5+s=3s5 + s = 3s5+s=3s, so 2s=52s = 52s=5 and s=2.5s = 2.5s=2.5 m.

  5. Answer (a) 5.4 m (b) 2.5 m

P30●●● AdvancedTrue/False with justification · 3 marksOriginal

True or false? "If two triangles have one pair of equal angles and two pairs of sides in the same ratio, they must be similar." Justify with an example.

Full solution

Given: a claim. Asked: true or false, with a reason and an example.

Concept used: SAS needs the angle between the sides; a counter-example disproves "must" (Topic 4). Why it applies: the claim does not say where the angle is.

  1. 1

    Take AB=5AB = 5AB=5 cm, AC=4AC = 4AC=4 cm and ∠B=40°\angle B = 40°∠B=40° (not between AB and AC).

  2. 2

    Two different triangles fit these facts: swing AC = 4 cm from A until it meets the 40° ray from B — it meets the ray at two points, C1C_1C1​ (with BC1≈6.21BC_1 \approx 6.21BC1​≈6.21 cm) and C2C_2C2​ (with BC2≈1.45BC_2 \approx 1.45BC2​≈1.45 cm).

  3. 3

    △ABC₁ has angles 40°, about 53.5° and about 86.5°; △ABC₂ has 40°, about 126.5° and about 13.5°. One triangle has an obtuse angle and the other has none, so no matching of their angles works: they are not similar.

  4. 4

    So the claim is false.

  5. Check: an accurate drawing shows that △ABC₁ has an acute angle at C1C_1C1​ (about 53.5°) while △ABC₂ has an obtuse angle at C2C_2C2​ (about 126.5°) — different shapes ✔.

  6. Answer False. SAS needs the equal angles to be included between the proportional sides; with AB=5AB = 5AB=5, AC=4AC = 4AC=4, ∠B=40°\angle B = 40°∠B=40° there are two different, non-similar triangles.

    Common trap: "True — it is SAS." Check that the angle is formed by the two sides.

If ∆ ABC ~ ∆ EDF and ∆ ABC is not similar to ∆ DEF, then which of the following is not true?

the matching card (Topic 4): A↔EA \leftrightarrow EA↔E, B↔DB \leftrightarrow DB↔D, C↔FC \leftrightarrow FC↔F, so ABED=BCDF=CAFE\dfrac{AB}{ED} = \dfrac{BC}{DF} = \dfrac{CA}{FE}EDAB​=DFBC​=FECA​. Why it applies: each option is a cross-multiplied ratio.

BC⋅EF=AC⋅FDBC \cdot EF = AC \cdot FDBC⋅EF=AC⋅FD means BCFD=ACEF\dfrac{BC}{FD} = \dfrac{AC}{EF}FDBC​=EFAC​ — true.
AB⋅EF=AC⋅DEAB \cdot EF = AC \cdot DEAB⋅EF=AC⋅DE means ABDE=ACEF\dfrac{AB}{DE} = \dfrac{AC}{EF}DEAB​=EFAC​ — true.
BC⋅DE=AB⋅EFBC \cdot DE = AB \cdot EFBC⋅DE=AB⋅EF means BCEF=ABDE\dfrac{BC}{EF} = \dfrac{AB}{DE}EFBC​=DEAB​ — but BC matches DF, not EF. Not true in general.
BC⋅DE=AB⋅FDBC \cdot DE = AB \cdot FDBC⋅DE=AB⋅FD means BCFD=ABDE\dfrac{BC}{FD} = \dfrac{AB}{DE}FDBC​=DEAB​ — true.

Given: △ABC ~ △EDF. Asked: the statement that is not true.

Concept used: the matching card (Topic 4): A↔EA \leftrightarrow EA↔E, B↔DB \leftrightarrow DB↔D, C↔FC \leftrightarrow FC↔F, so ABED=BCDF=CAFE\dfrac{AB}{ED} = \dfrac{BC}{DF} = \dfrac{CA}{FE}EDAB​=DFBC​=FECA​. Why it applies: each option is a cross-multiplied ratio.

  1. 1

    (A) BC⋅EF=AC⋅FDBC \cdot EF = AC \cdot FDBC⋅EF=AC⋅FD means BCFD=ACEF\dfrac{BC}{FD} = \dfrac{AC}{EF}FDBC​=EFAC​ — true.

  2. 2

    (B) AB⋅EF=AC⋅DEAB \cdot EF = AC \cdot DEAB⋅EF=AC⋅DE means ABDE=ACEF\dfrac{AB}{DE} = \dfrac{AC}{EF}DEAB​=EFAC​ — true.

  3. 3

    (D) BC⋅DE=AB⋅FDBC \cdot DE = AB \cdot FDBC⋅DE=AB⋅FD means BCFD=ABDE\dfrac{BC}{FD} = \dfrac{AB}{DE}FDBC​=DEAB​ — true.

  4. 4

    (C) BC⋅DE=AB⋅EFBC \cdot DE = AB \cdot EFBC⋅DE=AB⋅EF means BCEF=ABDE\dfrac{BC}{EF} = \dfrac{AB}{DE}EFBC​=DEAB​ — but BC matches DF, not EF. Not true in general.

    Reasoning for each option: (C) ✔ (the one that is not true); (A), (B), (D) ✘ each is a correct pairing.

  5. Check: the phrase "not similar to △DEF" warns you that the order DEF would be wrong ✔.

  6. Answer (C)

    Common trap: Pairing BC with EF because both are "the second and third letters" of different orders.
E2●● StandardMCQ · 1 markNCERT Exemplar Ch 6, Ex 6.1 Q4

If in two triangles ABC and PQR, ABQR=BCPR=CAPQ\dfrac{AB}{QR} = \dfrac{BC}{PR} = \dfrac{CA}{PQ}QRAB​=PRBC​=PQCA​, then

SSS and reading the matching from the ratios (Topic 4). Why it applies: AB ↔ QR, BC ↔ RP, CA ↔ PQ.

Given: the three side ratios. Asked: the correct similarity statement.

Concept used: SSS and reading the matching from the ratios (Topic 4). Why it applies: AB ↔ QR, BC ↔ RP, CA ↔ PQ.

  1. 1

    AB ↔ QR and BC ↔ RP share B and R: B↔RB \leftrightarrow RB↔R. Then A↔QA \leftrightarrow QA↔Q, C↔PC \leftrightarrow PC↔P.

  2. 2

    So △ABC ~ △QRP, which is the same as △PQR ~ △CAB (P ↔ C, Q ↔ A, R ↔ B).

    Reasoning for each option: (A) ✔. (B) pairs P with A; (C) pairs C with P correctly but B with Q; (D) pairs B with P.

  3. Check: in (A), PQ ↔ CA, QR ↔ AB, RP ↔ BC — exactly the given ratios ✔.

  4. Answer (A)

    Common trap: Choosing (B) because "all three ratios are equal, so they are similar in any order".

E4● FoundationMCQ · 1 markNCERT Exemplar Ch 6, Ex 6.1 Q7

In triangles ABC and DEF, ∠B = ∠E, ∠F = ∠C and AB = 3 DE. Then, the two triangles are

AA; congruent means scale factor 1 (Topics 2 and 4). Why it applies: the angles give similarity, the sides decide congruence.

Given: two pairs of equal angles; AB=3DEAB = 3DEAB=3DE. Asked: similar? congruent?

Concept used: AA; congruent means scale factor 1 (Topics 2 and 4). Why it applies: the angles give similarity, the sides decide congruence.

Full solution

Given: the four angles. Asked: is △QPR ~ △TSM?

Concept used: angle sum, AA, matching (Topic 4). Why it applies: the statement must pair equal angles.

  1. 1

    ∠R=180°−55°−25°=100°\angle R = 180° - 55° - 25° = 100°∠R=180°−55°−25°=100°; ∠T=180°−100°−25°=55°\angle T = 180° - 100° - 25° = 55°∠T=180°−100°−25°=55°.

    △QPR ~ △TSM would pair Q (25°) with T (55°) — false.

  4. Check: read △QPR ~ △STM back: 25° = 25°, 55° = 55°, 100° = 100° ✔.

  5. Answer No. The triangles are similar, but the correct statement is △QPR ~ △STM.

E10●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 6, Ex 6.2 Q7

Two sides and the perimeter of one triangle are respectively three times the corresponding sides and the perimeter of the other triangle. Are the two triangles similar? Why?

Full solution

Given: a′=3aa' = 3aa′=3a, b′=3bb' = 3bb′=3b and a′+b′+c′=3(a+b+c)a' + b' + c' = 3(a + b + c)a′+b′+c′=3(a+b+c). Asked: similar?

Concept used: SSS (Topic 4). Why it applies: we can find the third ratio.

  1. 1

    3a+3b+c′=3a+3b+3c3a + 3b + c' = 3a + 3b + 3c3a+3b+c′=3a+3b+3c.

  2. 2

    Subtract 3a+3b3a + 3b3a+3b: c′=3cc' = 3cc′=3c.

  3. 3

    All three sides are in the ratio 3, so the triangles are similar (SSS).

  4. Check: e.g. 3, 4, 5 and 9, 12, 15 ✔.

  5. Answer Yes — the third sides are also in the ratio 3 : 1, so SSS applies. (The Exemplar key's wording says the third sides "will also be equal"; it means equal in ratio — three times.)

    Common trap: Saying "only two sides are known, so we cannot tell" — the perimeter gives the third.

E21●●● AdvancedProof · 4 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 6, Ex 6.4 Q15

O is the point of intersection of the diagonals AC and BD of a trapezium ABCD with AB ∥ DC. Through O, a line segment PQ is drawn parallel to AB meeting AD in P and BC in Q. Prove that PO = QO.

Full solution

Given: AB∥DCAB \parallel DCAB∥DC; diagonals meet at O; PQ∥ABPQ \parallel ABPQ∥AB through O, P on AD, Q on BC. To prove: PO=QOPO = QOPO=QO.

Concept used: AA (corresponding angles) twice, and the trapezium ratio AOOC=BOOD\dfrac{AO}{OC} = \dfrac{BO}{OD}OCAO​=ODBO​ (Topics 4 and 5). Why it applies: PO and OQ are both parallel to DC.

  1. Statement Reason
    1. PQ∥DCPQ \parallel DCPQ∥DC PQ∥ABPQ \parallel ABPQ∥AB and AB∥DCAB \parallel DCAB∥DC
    2. △APO ~ △ADC, so PODC=AOAC\dfrac{PO}{DC} = \dfrac{AO}{AC}DCPO​=ACAO​ … (1) AA (corresponding angles, PO∥DCPO \parallel DCPO∥DC; common angle A)
    3. △BOQ ~ △BDC, so OQDC=BOBD\dfrac{OQ}{DC} = \dfrac{BO}{BD}DCOQ​=BDBO​ … (2) AA (corresponding angles, OQ∥DCOQ \parallel DCOQ∥DC; common angle B)
    4. AOOC=BOOD\dfrac{AO}{OC} = \dfrac{BO}{OD}OCAO​=ODBO​, so AOAC=BOBD\dfrac{AO}{AC} = \dfrac{BO}{BD}ACAO​=BDBO​ … (3) △OAB ~ △OCD (Topic 5); add 1 to the upside-down ratios
    5. PODC=OQDC\dfrac{PO}{DC} = \dfrac{OQ}{DC}DCPO​=DCOQ​ From (1), (2), (3)
    6. PO=OQPO = OQPO=OQ Multiply by DC. Hence proved.

  2. Check: in the trapezium of Topic 5, Worked example 6 (AB=12AB = 12AB=12, DC=8DC = 8DC=8), AOAC=35\dfrac{AO}{AC} = \dfrac{3}{5}ACAO​=53​, so PO=OQ=35×8=4.8PO = OQ = \dfrac{3}{5} \times 8 = 4.8PO=OQ=53​×8=4.8 cm ✔.

  3. Answer PO=QOPO = QOPO=QO.

    Common trap: Using △APO ~ △ADC for both halves. OQ lies in △BDC, which needs its own similarity.

E22●●● AdvancedShort answer · 3 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 6, Ex 6.4 Q9

In Fig. 6.18, ABC is a triangle right angled at B and BD ⊥ AC. If AD = 4 cm, and CD = 5 cm, find BD and AB.

(Figure, described: △ABC with the right angle at B; BD is drawn from B perpendicular to AC, meeting AC at D between A and C.)

Full solution

Given: ∠ABC=90°\angle ABC = 90°∠ABC=90°, BD⊥ACBD \perp ACBD⊥AC, AD=4AD = 4AD=4 cm, CD=5CD = 5CD=5 cm. Asked: BD and AB.

Concept used: the perpendicular from the right angle to the hypotenuse makes two triangles, each similar to the whole triangle and to each other (AA) (Topic 5). Why it applies: this is the same set-up as the 2026-27 sample-paper question for visually impaired candidates.

  1. Statement Reason
    1. In △ADB and △BDC: ∠ADB=∠BDC=90°\angle ADB = \angle BDC = 90°∠ADB=∠BDC=90° BD⊥ACBD \perp ACBD⊥AC
    2. ∠DAB=90°−∠ABD=∠DBC\angle DAB = 90° - \angle ABD = \angle DBC∠DAB=90°−∠ABD=∠DBC Angle sum in △ADB; and ∠ABD+∠DBC=∠ABC=90°\angle ABD + \angle DBC = \angle ABC = 90°∠ABD+∠DBC=∠ABC=90°
    3. △ADB ~ △BDC AA similarity criterion
    4. ADBD=BDCD\dfrac{AD}{BD} = \dfrac{BD}{CD}BDAD​=CDBD​, so BD2=AD×CD=4×5=20BD^2 = AD \times CD = 4 \times 5 = 20BD2=AD×CD=4×5=20 Corresponding sides of similar triangles are proportional
    5. BD=20=25BD = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}BD=20​=25​ cm A length is positive
    6. In △ADB and △ABC: ∠A\angle A∠A is common and ∠ADB=∠ABC=90°\angle ADB = \angle ABC = 90°∠ADB=∠ABC=90°, so △ADB ~ △ABC AA similarity criterion
    7. ADAB=ABAC\dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{AB}{AC}ABAD​=ACAB​, so AB2=AD×AC=4×9=36AB^2 = AD \times AC = 4 \times 9 = 36AB2=AD×AC=4×9=36 Corresponding sides proportional; AC=AD+DC=9AC = AD + DC = 9AC=AD+DC=9 cm
    8. AB=6AB = 6AB=6 cm A length is positive

  2. Check: in right △ADB, AD2+BD2=16+20=36=AB2AD^2 + BD^2 = 16 + 20 = 36 = AB^2AD2+BD2=16+20=36=AB2 ✔.

  3. Answer BD=25BD = 2\sqrt{5}BD=25​ cm; AB=6AB = 6AB=6 cm

    Common trap: Writing △ADB ~ △CDB (wrong order). Match the angles first: the angle at A in △ADB equals the angle DBC, so A ↔ B, D ↔ D, B ↔ C, giving △ADB ~ △BDC.

C1 — Case: Vijay's tower● FoundationCase/source-based · 5 marksCBSE Mathematics Class X Case Study Question Bank, Similar Triangles, Case Study 1

(Picture, described: Vijay's house on the left, a clock tower in the middle and Ajay's house on the right, each with its shadow on the ground and a sloping line for the sun's rays.)

Vijay is trying to find the average height of a tower near his house. He is using the properties of similar triangles.The height of Vijay's house if 20m when Vijay's house casts a shadow 10m long on the ground. At the same time, the tower casts a shadow 50m long on the ground and the house of Ajay casts 20m shadow on the ground.

  1. What is the height of the tower?

a) 20m b) 50m c) 100m d) 200m

  1. What will be the length of the shadow of the tower when Vijay's house casts a shadow of 12m?

a) 75m b) 50m c) 45m d) 60m

  1. What is the height of Ajay's house?

a) 30m b) 40m c) 50m d) 20m

  1. When the tower casts a shadow of 40m, same time what will be the length of the shadow of Ajay's house?

a) 16m b) 32m c) 20m d) 8m

  1. When the tower casts a shadow of 40m, same time what will be the length of the shadow of Vijay's house?

a) 15m b) 32m c) 16m d) 8m

(The bank writes "if 20m"; it means "is 20 m". "Average height" means simply the height.)

Full solution

Given: Vijay's house 20 m, shadow 10 m; tower's shadow 50 m; Ajay's house's shadow 20 m (same time). Asked: five answers.

Concept used: at one time, every height is the same multiple of its own shadow (Topic 5). Why it applies: the sun's rays make the same angle with the ground for all three buildings.

  1. 1

    At the first time: height = 2 × shadow (2010=2\dfrac{20}{10} = 21020​=2).

  2. 2

    Part 1: tower =2×50=100= 2 \times 50 = 100=2×50=100 m → (c).

  3. 3

    Part 2: Vijay's shadow 12 m means height = 2012×\dfrac{20}{12} \times1220​× shadow, so the tower's shadow is 100×1220=60100 \times \dfrac{12}{20} = 60100×2012​=60 m → (d).

  4. 4

    Part 3: Ajay's house =2×20=40= 2 \times 20 = 40=2×20=40 m → (b).

  5. 5

    Part 4: tower's shadow 40 m means height = 10040=2.5\dfrac{100}{40} = 2.540100​=2.5 × shadow; Ajay's shadow =402.5=16= \dfrac{40}{2.5} = 16=2.540​=16 m → (a).

  6. 6

    Part 5: Vijay's shadow =202.5=8= \dfrac{20}{2.5} = 8=2.520​=8 m → (d).

  7. Check: part 4 and part 5: 4016=208=2.5\dfrac{40}{16} = \dfrac{20}{8} = 2.51640​=820​=2.5 ✔.

  8. Answer

    1. (c) 100 m 2. (d) 60 m 3. (b) 40 m 4. (a) 16 m 5. (d) 8 m

    Common trap: In parts 2, 4 and 5 the sun has moved: use the new height-to-shadow ratio, not 2.

C2 — Case: a scale drawing of a train engine● FoundationCase/source-based · 3 marksCBSE Mathematics Class X Case Study Question Bank, Scale Factor case (questions 3, 4, 5)

A scale drawing of an object is the same shape at the object but a different size. The scale of a drawing is a comparison of the length used on a drawing to the length it represents. The scale is written as a ratio. The ratio of two corresponding sides in similar figures is called the scale factor

Scale factor= length in image / corresponding length in object

If one shape can become another using revising, then the shapes are similar. Hence, two shapes are similar when one can become the other after a resize, flip, slide or turn. In the photograph below showing the side view of a train engine. Scale factor is 1:200
This means that a length of 1 cm on the photograph above corresponds to a length of 200cm or 2 m, of the actual engine. The scale can also be written as the ratio of two lengths.

  1. What is the actual width of the door if the width of the door in photograph is 0.35cm?

a) 0.7m b) 0.7cm c) 0.07cm d) 0.07m

  1. If two similar triangles have a scale factor 5:3 which statement regarding the two triangles is true?

a) The ratio of their perimeters is 15:1 b) Their altitudes have a ratio 25:15 c) Their medians have a ratio 10:4 d) Their angle bisectors have a ratio 11:5

  1. The length of AB in the given figure:

a) 8cm b) 6cm c) 4cm d) 10cm

(Figure for question 5, described: a right triangle ADE with the right angle at D and DE = 6 cm along the bottom; B is on AD with BD = 4 cm and AB = x cm; BC is drawn parallel to DE, with the right angle at B, and BC = 3 cm; C is on AE.)

(The bank's questions 1 and 2 are left out: question 1 mixes up the model and the photograph, and the key to question 2 picks "they are not the mirror image of one another" as what affects similarity — but flips do not affect similarity, as the passage itself says. "the same shape at the object" means "as the object"; "revising" means "resizing".)

Full solution

Given: scale 1 : 200; a door 0.35 cm wide in the photograph; scale factor 5 : 3; the figure for question 5. Asked: three answers.

Concept used: actual length = 200 × photo length; every length in similar triangles is in the scale factor; BPT / similar triangles for the figure (Topics 2, 3, 5). Why it applies: BC ∥ DE (both perpendicular to AD).

  1. 1

    Q3: 0.35×200=700.35 \times 200 = 700.35×200=70 cm =0.7= 0.7=0.7 m → (a).

  2. 2

    Q4: altitudes are in the side ratio: 25:15=5:325 : 15 = 5 : 325:15=5:3 → (b). ((a) 15:115 : 115:1, (c) 10:4=5:210 : 4 = 5 : 210:4=5:2 and (d) 11:511 : 511:5 are not 5:35 : 35:3.)

  3. 3

    Q5: △ABC ~ △ADE (AA: right angles at B and D, common angle A), so ABAD=BCDE\dfrac{AB}{AD} = \dfrac{BC}{DE}ADAB​=DEBC​: xx+4=36\dfrac{x}{x + 4} = \dfrac{3}{6}x+4x​=63​.

  4. 4

    Cross-multiply: 6x=3x+126x = 3x + 126x=3x+12, so x=4x = 4x=4 → (c).

  5. Check: Q5: AD=8AD = 8AD=8, and 48=36\dfrac{4}{8} = \dfrac{3}{6}84​=63​ ✔.

  6. Answer

    1. (a) 0.7 m 4. (b) 5. (c) 4 cm

    Common trap: Q5: ABBD=BCDE\dfrac{AB}{BD} = \dfrac{BC}{DE}BDAB​=DEBC​ (part-to-part against whole sides) gives x=2x = 2x=2 cm.
